title: The Puritans in America
summary: Josh and Chuck (with iHeart Intro co-host voice) explore the Puritans: their origins as extreme English Protestants shaped by Calvinism and the upheavals of 1530s-1660s England, the Separatists and Pilgrims, the founding of the Massachusetts Bay Colony under John Winthrop, the Massachusetts Bay Company, life in colonial New England (church, schooling, the Old Deluder Satan Act, Harvard), Puritan attitudes toward dress, sex, drinking, and women, dissenters Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson, persecution of Quakers, the Pequot War and the enslavement of Pequots, the Puritan legacy in America, and a listener email at the end.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts open the show with light banter about the episode and the Puritans.

segments.title: Who were the Puritans
segments.summary: Puritans were extreme Protestants who wanted to purify the Church of England; their formation came from upheaval in England from the 1530s to 1660s, leading some to separate and move to Holland and North America.

segments.title: Separatists, Calvinism and the word Puritan
segments.summary: Separatists left in 1608 and later founded Plymouth; the Puritans followed Calvinist predestination; the term Puritan began as an insult.

segments.title: Praying directly to God and church authority
segments.summary: Puritans disputed whether believers could pray directly to God or needed church officials; they opposed church money demands and held elitist views tied to wealth.

segments.title: Pilgrims, Plymouth and Christmas
segments.summary: The Separatists settled at Plymouth with about a hundred people; the hosts note Puritans disliked Christmas.

segments.title: Massachusetts Bay Colony and the Pilgrim difference
segments.summary: The Massachusetts Bay Colony was founded in 1630 under John Winthrop; Puritans and Pilgrims were separate groups, with the Pilgrims more radical separatists and the Puritans better funded.

segments.title: Watching one another for Satan
segments.summary: Puritans believed Satan actively tempted people, so community and family members watched each other closely for signs of corruption.

segments.title: The Witch film aside
segments.summary: Brief digression on the film The Witch and a word-search tangent.

segments.title: Massachusetts Bay Company finances
segments.summary: The colony was founded by the Massachusetts Bay Company, a stock venture trading fur and fish; voting shareholders were colony residents, letting Puritans keep control.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Early Massachusetts government and expansion
segments.summary: Winthrop was repeatedly re-elected under annual elections; Boston was founded; settlements spread to Rhode Island and Maine; King Charles I dissolved Parliament in 1629 and about 20,000 Puritans emigrated by 1640.

segments.title: English civil war migrants and economic growth
segments.summary: Scottish, Irish, English and French immigrants arrived during the English civil war period, boosting the colony's economy with craftsmen and merchants; Connecticut was founded by John Hooker; Rhode Island by Puritan dissidents.

segments.title: Plymouth absorbed and early schooling
segments.summary: Plymouth struggled and was absorbed into Massachusetts in 1691; the Puritans emphasized church and schooling, so everyone could read the Bible.

segments.title: Old Deluder Satan Act and Harvard
segments.summary: The 1647 Old Deluder Satan Act required towns to hire schoolmasters or build grammar schools; the college founded in 1636 was renamed Harvard after John Harvard's bequest, and the town became Cambridge.

segments.title: Dress, sex and marriage among Puritans
segments.summary: Puritans later allowed displays of wealth in clothing; they did not oppose sex within marriage and tolerated premarital sex with pregnancy requiring marriage; the Scarlet Letter was a real practice.

segments.title: Puritan drinking
segments.summary: Puritans drank heavily, about twice the per-capita pure alcohol of modern Americans (six gallons in 1790 versus 2.83 gallons in 2021).

segments.title: Women and Puritan society
segments.summary: Women had few legal rights but some led sermons or had influence in churches; they were respected for domestic work and childbirth; the Salem witch trials were an exceptional incident.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Roger Williams and Rhode Island
segments.summary: Roger Williams was ousted for outspokenness, favored separation of church and state and fair dealings with Native Americans, bought land from the Narragansett, and founded Rhode Island as a haven for non-Puritans; he converted to Baptism in 1639.

segments.title: Anne Hutchinson banishment
segments.summary: Anne Hutchinson, a midwife, was excommunicated for her outspoken views on direct connection to the Holy Spirit, moved to Rhode Island with her family, and was joined there by Williams.

segments.title: Persecution of Quakers
segments.summary: Massachusetts persecuted Quakers, hanging four including Mary Dyer; in 1661 King Charles II ordered an end to the killings.

segments.title: Puritan hypocrisy
segments.summary: Puritans were seen as hypocritical for persecuting others after suffering persecution in England; their elitism clashed with Quaker egalitarianism.

segments.title: Slavery, the Pequot War and Massachusetts
segments.summary: After epidemics in 1620, colonists took land as God's design; the Pequot War led to enslavement of Pequots sent to the West Indies to trade for Africans; only a few hundred enslaved people were in the colonies, far fewer than in the South.

segments.title: Decline of Puritanism and its legacy
segments.summary: Puritanism gradually declined as society became more open-minded; England cracked down on colonial independence in the 1680s; the hosts discuss lasting Puritan influences such as work ethic, education and intolerance.

segments.title: Temperance and Mencken quote
segments.summary: Descendants of the Puritans took aim at alcohol in the Great Awakening; H. L. Mencken's line that Puritanism is the haunting fear someone may be happy is quoted.

segments.title: Listener email from Nelson
segments.summary: A listener writes about the family's appreciation for the show, including hospital visits and the audio book; the hosts invite the family to a Chicago show as guests.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts encourage listeners to send mail and note the show is an iHeartRadio production.
